structured_output.summary:
I searched outside sources for evidence on the open hypotheses, mainly H2.1 (progressive resizing). E006 showed it gives the best accuracy-for-time trade so far. Findings:

(1) The reference recipe already uses dirac init. Its Conv.reset_parameters calls nn.init.dirac_, which matches the 45 ms dirac loop seen in profiling. H1.2's premise is wrong, so H1.2.1 should be dropped.

(2) The architecture constrains which resolutions work. Rough check from the published code: the 2x2 whitening conv has no padding and is followed by three MaxPool2d(2) and a final MaxPool2d(3). So 32 px goes 31→15→7→3, and 26, 28 or 30 px also end at a 3x3 grid. 24 px ends at 2x2, which degrades or breaks the final 3x3 pool. 26 px may be a better low-res stage than 24.

(3) Published schedules spend much longer at full resolution than E006 did (about 22%):
- EfficientTrain++: 20% of training at 0.43x scale, 40% at 0.71x, last 40% at full resolution.
- FFCV: ramps up late and keeps roughly the last 30% at maximum resolution.
- Composer defaults: final 20% at full resolution.
- Composer reports random crops working better than resizing for CIFAR, and EfficientTrain++ reports low-frequency (Fourier) cropping beating plain downsampling. E006's random-resized downsampling is therefore a likely cause of its −0.69 pp loss. FixRes describes the train/test apparent-object-size mismatch that resize-based low-res training creates.

(4) Fable's 24→28→32 px schedule was the main real speedup on CIFAR-10 at matched 94% accuracy: −7.6%, from 1.978 s to 1.828 s.

(5) Hiverge's exact color jitter is brightness ±0.14 and contrast ±0.13 (H1.4). Its SiLU, batch size 1536 and label smoothing 0.09 were tuned for CIFAR-10, and E003 already showed SiLU hurts on CIFAR-100.

(6) The futurebiohackers PR supports two things:
- H5: Muon lost to SGD at every size.
- The epoch–accuracy slope near 8.5 epochs is flat: 9 epochs gave about +0.1 pp for +6% time. That is lower than the notebook's 0.3–0.5 pp/epoch estimate.

(7) The reference learning-rate schedule warms up over 23% of steps from 0.2x and decays to 0.07x, not to zero. Budgeted-training results (Li et al., ICLR 2020) and airbench94_muon both use linear decay to zero, which is an untested lever. Cutout is 0 in the reference.

(8) For H3.3, airbench94_muon uses batch size 2000, 8 epochs, wd = 2e-6 × batch size and linear decay. Hiverge uses 1536.

(9) For H2.3, airbench96_faster's proxy-based filtering cut CIFAR-10 time from 34.7 s to 27.3 s, but over 45 epochs. Its overhead pattern (a separate proxy net, filtering every 4 steps) is unproven at around 8 epochs.

findings.claim: The reference Conv class already applies dirac init in reset_parameters: `nn.init.dirac_(w[: w.size(1)])`, covering the first in_channels filters. The airbench paper credits identity init with about 2.2 epochs saved on CIFAR-10, and that gain is already in the recipe.
findings.relevance: H1.2 assumes the reference lacks dirac init, which is false. 'Add dirac and cut 1 epoch' has no mechanism. Retire H1.2/H1.2.1 or reframe them, e.g. extending dirac to all output filters.

findings.claim: Architecture geometry: the whitening conv is nn.Conv2d(3,24,kernel_size=2,padding=0), each group ends in MaxPool2d(2), and the head uses MaxPool2d(3) before the linear layer. Defaults: widths [128,384,576], translate 2, cutout 0, scaling_factor 1/9, 5000 whitening images. Derived spatial chain: 32→31→15→7→3; 30→29→14→7→3; 28→27→13→6→3; 26→25→12→6→3; 24→23→11→5→2. 24 px leaves a 2x2 map, smaller than the final 3x3 pool window.
findings.relevance: Within H2.1, 26 px (FLOPs about 0.66x of 32) keeps the head's 3x3 pooling geometry, where 24 px (about 0.56x) does not. Part of E006's −0.69 pp may come from the 24 px stage's degenerate final pool. A 26→(28/30)→32 schedule is a natural next test.

findings.claim: EfficientTrain++ schedule: 0–20% of the budget at 96/224 (0.43x), 20–60% at 160/224 (0.71x), 60–100% at full resolution. Low-frequency (Fourier-domain) cropping beats plain downsampling (their Table XIX(b)). Training on low-pass data tracks the baseline early and diverges only midway, and 50–75% of training can drop high frequencies without final accuracy loss. The paper reports 1.5–3x wall-time savings on ImageNet.
findings.relevance: E006 kept only about 22% of epochs at full resolution (7–8 of 9). Published schedules keep about 40% at full resolution and push the cheapest stage early. Switching from bilinear or random-resized downsampling to antialiased or FFT low-pass resizing may recover accuracy at the same FLOPs.

findings.claim: MosaicML Composer progressive resizing defaults: initial_scale 0.5, delay_fraction 0.5, finetune_fraction 0.2 (last 20% at full resolution), linear ramp between, sizes snapped to multiples of 4. Its 'crop' mode (random crop at the smaller size, no rescaling) beat 'resize' for ResNet-56 on CIFAR-10, 'where the objects are similar sizes to one another and the images are already low resolution'.
findings.relevance: This is a direct CIFAR-specific hint that E006's random-resized crops may be the wrong low-res operator. Random 24–28 px crops keep object scale identical to test-time 32 px. Testing crop mode against resize mode at the same schedule is a cheap A/B.

findings.claim: FixRes (Touvron et al., NeurIPS 2019): a mismatch in apparent object size between train-time augmentation and test-time preprocessing hurts accuracy. Fine-tuning the classifier plus the last BatchNorm at the test resolution fixes most of it cheaply, with no full backprop needed.
findings.relevance: Mechanism behind the accuracy cost of resize-based low-res training: downscaled images show smaller objects than test images. It supports keeping a full-resolution tail. A cheaper option is a very short final phase at 32 px with frozen early layers, which recalibrates BN and head statistics.

findings.claim: FFCV ImageNet ResNet-50 configs hold the minimum resolution (160) for most of training, ramp linearly to the maximum (192) late (roughly the last 30%), then evaluate at 224, above the maximum training resolution. Resolution is a linear interpolation between start_ramp and end_ramp epochs.
findings.relevance: Another strong recipe keeps low resolution long but puts the full-resolution phase at the end with a ramp, not abrupt steps. This supports trying a smooth 26→32 ramp with a longer full-resolution tail.

findings.claim: On CIFAR-10 (94% target), Fable's main legitimate speedup was progressive resizing 24→28→32 px, plus pooling, CUDA-graph and optimizer-fusion work. Net real gain was −7.6% vs the Hiverge SOTA (1.978→1.828 s). The writeup gives no epoch fractions or interpolation details.
findings.relevance: Independent confirmation that progressive resizing transfers to airbench-style nets at matched accuracy. A realistic matched-accuracy gain is likely below E006's −18.6%: perhaps 8–12% after compensating epochs.

findings.claim: Ablation table (A100, CIFAR-100): airbench94 12 ep 70.6%/3.5 s; airbench96 (3 convs) 12 ep 76.0%/9.4 s; 9 ep/576 75.6%/8.58 s; 8 ep/768 75.6%/8.40 s; 8.5 ep/576 75.5%/8.11 s. Going 8.5→9 epochs adds about +0.1 pp for +6% time. Muon 'lost to SGD at every size, so it was removed'. Label smoothing 0.3 beat 0.2 and 0.4. About 95% of GPU time is in conv, BN and GELU kernels.
findings.relevance: Supports H5/H5.1.1 (Muon worse). The accuracy-per-epoch slope near 8.5 epochs looks about 0.1–0.2 pp per 0.5 epoch, flatter than the notebook's 0.3–0.5 pp/epoch estimate. Recovering E006's −0.69 pp by adding epochs alone may take more than 1 extra epoch, so schedule shape and resize operator matter more. Their 8 ep/768 = 75.6% contrasts with our E005 (7.5 ep/768 = 75.13%), which suggests a steep accuracy cliff below 8 epochs.

findings.claim: LR schedule: warmup over the first 23% of steps from 0.2x to full LR, then decay to 7% of the initial LR at the last step. Lookahead-EMA every 5 steps with decay 0.95**5 * (t/T)**3. Momentum 0.85 Nesterov, wd 0.012 per 1024 examples. No TTA in eval.
findings.relevance: New, untested direction: the LR schedule ends at 0.07x, not zero. Budgeted-training results favor linear decay to zero at a fixed budget (next finding). Schedules must be re-derived when the epoch count or resolution phases change.

findings.claim: Budgeted Training (Li, Yumer, Ramanan, ICLR 2020): with a fixed iteration budget, the LR schedule must be tuned to the budget. Simple linear decay to zero is robust and high-performing across ImageNet, Kinetics, COCO and Cityscapes. The paper credits 'budgeted convergence' (gradient vanishing at the end of the budget) for good schedules.
findings.relevance: Suggests testing decay to 0 (instead of 0.07x) and possibly a shorter warmup. This is a zero-cost accuracy lever that could buy the ~0.2–0.7 pp slack needed to cut epochs or keep progressive resizing.

findings.claim: Hiverge CIFAR-10 record (94.02%, 1.98 s): batch size 1536, 7.65 epochs, label smoothing 0.09, SiLU, Muon lr 0.205 with momentum 0.655, SGD momentum 0.825, wd 1.0418e-6*bs. Per-batch color jitter: brightness_shift = U(-1,1)*0.1399, contrast_scale = 1 + U(-1,1)*0.1308. Flip plus pad-2 translate.
findings.relevance: Gives concrete jitter magnitudes for H1.4.1 (start around brightness 0.14 and contrast 0.13, maybe smaller given CIFAR-100's label smoothing 0.3). The SiLU result does not transfer (E003 refuted it on CIFAR-100). Batch size 1536 is a data point for H3.3.

findings.claim: airbench94_muon: batch_size 2000, 8 epochs, bias_lr 0.053, head_lr 0.67, Muon lr 0.24 with momentum 0.6, SGD momentum 0.85 Nesterov, wd = 2e-6*batch_size, label smoothing 0.2. Whitening bias trains for 3 epochs. LR is linear decay 1 - step/total_steps, down to zero.
findings.relevance: Batch-size reference for H3.3.1: airbench went to bs 2000 with wd scaled by batch size and linear decay to zero. Also a second data point favoring a decay-to-zero schedule.

findings.claim: airbench96_faster reaches 96.00% in 27.3 s vs airbench96's 96.03% in 34.7 s (−21%) via data filtering. A small proxy net (widths 32/64/64, depth 2) picks the top 512 by loss from each 1024-image batch. The baseline trains for about 45 epochs, and TTA level 2 is used.
findings.relevance: Selective-backprop gains are shown only for long (45-epoch) CIFAR-10 runs with a separate proxy. At about 8 epochs on 500 images per class, the proxy's forward cost and the reduced sample coverage likely eat the gain. This supports keeping H2.3 at low priority.

findings.claim: airbench ablations (CIFAR-10, from a 21-epoch whitened baseline): identity init about −2.2 epochs, BN-bias 64x LR about −1.7, lookahead about −0.5, multi-crop TTA about −0.4, alternating flip about −0.4; torch.compile gave a 14% wall-clock speedup. Alternating flip helped in every setting tested. airbench96 on CIFAR-100 without retuning reached 79.27% (79.76% with Cutout).
findings.relevance: Every trick from this list that is allowed is already in the reference (TTA is banned). Remaining gains must come from new levers (resolution schedule, LR shape, augmentation), not from airbench's known tricks.
